    AI Overview
    There are 38 federally recognized Native American tribes headquartered in Oklahoma. The largest, the Cherokee Nation, has over 450,000 citizens. Other major nations with significant, sovereign, and, following the 2020 McGirt v. Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling, reservation lands include the Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee (Creek), and Seminole Nations. 
    Key details regarding major nations in Oklahoma include: 
    • Cherokee Nation: Based in Tahlequah, it is the largest tribe in the US, covering 16 counties in northeastern Oklahoma.
    • Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma: Headquartered in Durant, it covers 10.5 counties in southeastern Oklahoma.
    • Chickasaw Nation:
      Located in south-central Oklahoma with headquarters in Ada.
    • Muscogee Nation: Based in Okmulgee, representing the Muscogee (Creek) people.
    • Seminole Nation of Oklahoma: Located in Seminole County.
    • Osage Nation: Headquartered in Pawhuska. 
    Many other tribes exist throughout the state, including the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, and Delaware Nation. These tribes have a massive economic impact on the state and provide health, education, and social services to their citizens.

    What color eyes do Cherokee have?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Cherokee people primarily have brown eyes, which is the dominant eye color among indigenous populations. Due to historic and ongoing intermarriage with European settlers, varied eye colors—including hazel, green, and blue—exist within the Cherokee population today. While some legends mention light-eyed individuals, these are generally not considered representative of the ancestral population. 
    • Dominant Features: Traditionally, Cherokee individuals have dark brown eyes, black hair, and darker skin pigmentation.
    • Diversity: Modern Cherokee citizens exhibit a wide range of physical traits, from very fair to very dark skin, and black to blond or red hair, and blue or light eyes.
    • Blue Eyes: While rare in pre-Columbian Native Americans, blue eyes are found in some Cherokee individuals today, often due to European admixture.
    • Legend of "Moon-Eyed" People: Cherokee oral tradition includes stories of the "Moon-eyed people," described as a small, white-skinned group with large blue eyes. However, this is largely treated as folklore rather than a documentation of ancestral Cherokee traits.
    • Genetic Studies: Research indicates that ancient and contemporary Native Americans are predicted to have intermediate or brown eyes.
